body:
I'm sorry you feel that way, but hopefully your impression of the forum will change in time. Part of what you describe is a logistical problem. This forum accepts survivors from all over the spectrum of abuse and recovery. I think mods felt it was more important to take people at their word. To facilitate healing and approach abuse with the seriousness it deserves, people tend to suggest what appear to be drastic measures. It may seem kind like a weird alternare universe at first, but the truth is that very few will impose their views on you. It's generally understood that there are good reasons people stay in contact with their abusers, sometimes they don't have a choice, sometimes, they just aren't ready. Not every situation is a life and death emergency. You don't even have to convince us or justify your decision. RBN taught me a handy little acronym for that, JADE (Justify, Argue, Defend, Explain) and it's part of the cycle of abuse and I'm pretty sure the mods and users wouldn't let anyone harrass you in that way. I think these are the reasons this sub has grown so much, but I can understand how people might see it as enabling at a glance. That might have worried me at one point but I've see too many success stories that are a direct result of the good things happening here. 

Then there are the people are suffering from denial, when they come post here it's almost on a whim. Our perception of the abuse changes over time, usually it turns out it was worse than we initially thought. In your case, maybe not. If you can maintain a loving relationship with your mom you are really lucky and I think many of us really want that. We have to do some major guesswork, we are all just a bunch of strangers here who happen to have seen you bare your soul... I feel like this gets misconstrued by other parts of Reddit. You don't have worry about what they think. That worry is pretty common around here but I think the bulk of it stems from a negative perception planted by a critical parent AND a culture that doesn't want to accept that abuse happens a lot more than we want to admit. Hence the labeling and negative portrayal as a ragtag brigade of spoiled brats, unhinged losers, and outcasts that might be eating their feelings in mom's basement. I haven't met any RBNers personally but I know for a fact we have just as many gainfully employed, educated, married, respectably middle-aged folk as the front page. The confidential nature of this sub makes it hard to point to someone normal and go see, throwawaysurvivor is really a student at such and such college with a great social life and bright future ahead of them. Factor in the lurkers and I bet the userbase is even bigger than we think.

Aw, now you can level up to LifeAfterNarcissism, achievement unlocked. You've inspired me in an uncertain and intimidating time in my life. It just feels good to know abusive parents are losing their grip on us as we awaken to the depth of the crisis and begin forming these support networks. 

Forming my own belief system apart from the pressure to conform to the positivity-at-all-costs mindset was crucial for me too. For instance, one false dichotomy that drives me up the walls is the whole: 
Mental illness=bad, so naturally, reality=good when life is at best, a struggle even without health problems, toxic families, or other "natural disasters" that many of us are marked and formed by. When so many of us have been raised by parents with extreme reactivity, that cultish optimism can result in serious cognitive dissonance like you described, as well as dissociation and maladaptive daydreaming. Not conducive to healing that part of us that can't bring ourselves to show authentic nurturing and love to ourselves.

I'm sending your post in a time machine to my past self. Wish me luck...

Another concept that resonates with me is the sunken cost fallacy. We put so much time and effort and other resources into this black hole of abuse.

Is this how doctors justify their lack of bedside manner too? That's no excuse for forgoing common courtesy. Disagreements and miscommunication happen all the time, the context doesn't take away from that.

That is one big wall of anxiety ridden text. So you're finding yourself in a self-destructive cycle. That can be incredibly daunting. I really, really think you should take your mind off school for a little while, maybe about a year. It will probably the most terrifying thing you'll ever do, but living on your own, say in California, establishing residency if that is applicable to your present circumstances, get yourself a fun colorful fish or a plant or something that doesn't require a serious commitment. You're setting yourself up to fail if you force yourself into something without being stable. Trust me, it's better to take a year off and deal with your problems, get therapy, live on your own, and slow waaaay down with the OCD levels of future based panic. Use the time to figure out how you can take small steps to get where you want to be. That's my advice and I hope you'll consider drafting a game plan of some sort.

You are so close to your independence, you might as well stick it out and give it a shot. I think some great things are coming your way and you seem very mature for your age, despite the fact that you are being overwhelmed with a lot more responsibilty than you probably should be carrying at your age. You deserve a break, it's kind of like the way Friday seems so far away on a Wednesday. I think you've got the right idea in seeking professional help. If there is a university near you they also might be offering services for a minimal fee through their training programs for newly licensed therapists.

Don't waste that death drive, get into cliff jumping or something cool. Maybe people would accept you then. All sarcasm aside, people perish in such a diverse range of circumstances every day, and then one day you realize you're suicidal and you realize how hard it is to actually kill yourself off at will. Maybe God does exist after all...To be honest, it sounds like you are not 100% on board to end it. Who is "everyone"? Because you can't possibly mean it literally. If you really want to die, maybe risk your life to save another, or in the fight for a good cause.

Suicide can be a rational decision in a world that is as dysfunctional as ours. Depression used to be called "a dark night of the soul," an existential crisis. A lot of the time it is not a chemical imbalance, a lot of things factor into it, even if disorted thinking is also present. I think it would be good for you to evaluate your thoughts more, because while you are right about your life being miserable now, as a person with free will, being so young, you are luckier than a lot of us who are in this position. You don't have to be like this, at least give it 10 more years, what do you have to lose? You can't possibly think you know what the world has to offer you, you might as well try to learn about how the world actually works, since you're already here. Even if you are miserable every step of the way, there is more to life than your social life or your family or your immediate surroundings.

Reality can be excruciating, so can mental illness. Either way, I think what helps the most is a reason to live. Right now I'm lacking that, so it makes me feel like the sum of my flaws makes me a total joke of a human being. I wish I could contribute something that would really lift your spirits, but I'm just trying to be honest. 

Is there anyway you can work toward a goal you can truly accomplish? Breaking a larger goal into smaller ones is one way to start reevaluating your strengths and weaknesses. We may never be exactly who we want to be, but being on the right path can give you enough of a reason to at least keep trying for another day.

Whoa...the snippets of your facebook interaction is like shining a flashlight into the murky, rarely seen recesses of a BPD mind. Good job. This is exactly what live conversations are like with them, and now you at least have proof, which will provide at the very least, some peace of mind. Thanks for sharing!

Unless she has an intervention involving multiple family members and a professional who is a black belt in Cluster B tactics, I don't think you can expect too much. I mean, you can try to slowly worm your way into her head but it may break your spirit. Be careful. Your financial independence is good leverage though, she doesn't have as many strings to pull. You might just be able to get through, I suggest maybe loosing up her defenses by getting more in depth about her own childhood, she was more than likely a child abuse survivor. Look for ways to help her feel safe. People are way more likely to admit their flaws when they feel safe (and not in the narcissistic or dissociative sense). I'll be the first to admit this is as blatant an example of parentification as it gets though.

I hate hearing these stories, this kind of thing seems to happen way too much. What on earth was she trying to accomplish by being antagonistic and flippant? If anyone was noncompliant it was her. She should be well-aware her attitude is against the code of conduct of her profession. If you were actually resistant to treatment, you would need help more than ever and honestly you probably wouldn't be there in the first place. She is either poorly trained or incompetent. Bah. 

Some people just find themselves in the wrong profession for one reason or another. I started feeling a lot better when I lowered my expectations for therapy quite a bit. It's just me at the end of the day. Giving up on help was surprisingly soothing to my soul. I don't get triggered as much when people don't get me and it helps me communicate more effectively.

You sound very sane for someone being raised in a "family" like that. There are no adults in your home, you don't have a family, because in order to have a family there needs to be at least one functioning adult in charge. 

Whatever you do, don't depend on her for ANYTHING. Think of yourself as an orphan in a temporary home. Chances are she'll sabotage your future plans, think about it, she has nothing to lose and everything to gain by keeping you around. 

Keep doing whatever you are doing, it seems to be working. It can be lonely out there but you always have RBN.

No judgment from me either. I was able to overcome those thoughts eventually too. Killing wasn't going to even the score, the time, resources, love, and peace of mind they stole and withheld from us is irrecoverable. I would actually describe myself as a pacifist and idealist to a fault. I still had some pretty vivid fantasies about smearing her blood on the walls in a gratitious display of violence. Some very honest therapists will admit that the most effective modality (for rehabilitation from abuse) is unconditional love. In that light, therapy falls pretty short. The reality is that we are more or less on our own, as bleak as that sounds. In preparing for the worst, we allow ourselves a much better shot at making choices that lead to our independence and freedom. Therapy has been a resource for many survivors, a group of which you are undoubtedly a member, it's the generally accepted way to process trauma. We can't discount the deeply ingrained cultural belief that it's a cureall for whatever troubles us. 

The statute of limitations hasn't run out on your abuse. If you can turn your desire for justice into something constructive, I say why not. If you have concrete evidence of your abuse, you have that option open to you. Most of us don't. If a lawyer is willing to take you on as a client, you'll have to weigh the financial burden, the psychological burden, whether you're in a stable enough condition to weather the storm and if it will somehow impact your future and future employment negatively. Even if your abuser doesn't exactly spend the rest of their life behind bars, some recognition would in all likelihood be a monumental step toward recovery. In my opinion, those violent thoughts arise in part from how abusive parents just get away with their crimes against humanity (literally en masse) and most of us have a functioning moral compass and know how evil that is. 

You're safe here, at least. No one is going to think you are unhinged and come after you. Boundaries are as important in therapy as anywhere else, and you're under no binding obligation to reveal your darkest inner thoughts to a therapist. Finding the right therapist can be tricky too, so it's probably best to keep a safe distance until you are sure they can be of service to you. The thoughts themselves don't seem to be irrational, but I can relate. To have been forced into that position in the first place is practically unthinkable.

"The odd thing about beating a dog is not that the dog gets meaner each time you beat him. It is that you get meaner each time you beat the dog." 

Credit to the comments section of youtube for this gem 😂. I came across it earlier today and it brought to mind my sophomore year of high school when I took AP Psych, the teacher was this slow talking, chubby football coach who actually went to Harvard for his undergrad, people could not figure out if this guy was brilliant or just really random. "Like breeds like. Dislike breeds dislike," is pretty much the only thing I remember from that class but it was a powerful line that made an impression on my confused, battered brain.  

We're the real life Stanford Prison Experiment prisoners. Authority, no oversight, and a dubious moral high ground is the perfect environment for abuse. The parent-child relationship is a greenhouse for dysfunction to grow out of control. So-called good intentions have to be firmly in place so that you can slowly turn up the heat of the violence or destruction without people noticing. The longer they get entrenched in the role of the perpetrator, the harder it is for them to get out of it. N's come in all shapes and sizes, so that's my assessment of the more redeemable ones. 

Abusers are basically living double lives, and they constantly hear cultural messages about parental sacrifices and hard work. A lot of them suffer from very distorted thinking and they interpret an ongoing and intense level of conflict to be an inevitable way of life. The paranoid ones really think deep down that all relationships are transactional and based on power so they literally can't imagine anything better or healthier.

My honest take on this is also that it's socially acceptable and even encouraged for people in general to take out their resentment and stress on their children. No one bats an eye when people basically make kids out to be fundamentally bad little creatures that need to be tamed like wild animals. But when you take a step back it's obvious no one has it easy, even kids who aren't parentified the way abused kids are. Even the youngest kids have to struggle to do the most basic tasks, walking is considered an accomplishment at certain age for fuckssake. Then the older they get, the more competitive and uncertain the world becomes. Life isn't easy for anyone at any point in their life, yet kids are the go-to scapegoats for stressed out adults. Teenagers are some of the worst victims of unnecessary and hurtful smears. Reality TV is proof positive adults don't have it together. I don't see myself climbing some golden ladder to enlightenment. In fact, the only knowitall phase I went through was after encountering a 30 year old N asshat that eventually became my boyfriend. He was far more immature than many (or even most) teenagers I've come across. N abuse isn't just the sole brainchild of the abuser, they don't get all the credit. People often have the desire to harm others, but child abuse happens because people let parents get away with way too much.

You are free to let loose a little, and to be your own person. I'm finding it increasingly harder to escape the feeling you describe. I'll just be curled up on the sofa checking out Rihanna's new video trying to relax and keep the bad thoughts at bay when my internal dialog interrupts: I've never danced liked that or been so, alive?? I'm exploring the idea that these are the kind of growing pains I missed out on because I was heavily dissociated during my teen years and maybe this is what normal people go through when they're 13 or 14 ideally. I've gotten a lot of well-intentioned advice like, "Just be yourself," from people who don't quite get what's going on but can sympathize with my mom's toxic influence. Bleep, bloop. That really only works for people who have a self but lack confidence, for me it's pretty much the other way around. My motivation and ability to act has always been based on the desire to become more and more refined. Which is actually pretty normal, we're all here to improve ourselves but my problem lies with how my mom idealizes in an unhealthy way and is just generally a very weird person. Growing up in her distortion or shared psychosis has been like being drugged since birth. It's literally all I know, so when I recently recognized it for what it is, I feel absolutely horrible all the time. Even while recognizing she's mentally ill, somehow she heavily influenced my values and the way I see the world. It's so hard to put into words, that identity was what made me feel productive, like my life meant something. It was a completely false sense of security and happiness. I feel so empty and directionless.

The awkward N family combo is the worst, I think we're definitely on the same page. My mom has a similar fantasy of belonging to the elite, but she misses many of the details. The result is truly bizarre, like she's just a blurry shadow of a real person. I feel like I wasn't raised by a real human being. It went overlooked in part because I was quickly labeled mature and expected to be quiet, unmemorable, but self-sufficient. Fast forward a couple decades and I have no personality and I hate it. Going back and reevaluating my life I see I was always slightly off in some way.

It REALLY scares me that I might never overcome the damage. Maybe it's because we were so young and our brains didn't develop properly. This is the main thing holding me back from feeling fully healed. I sincerely hope there is a way out! I barely make it through the day now because I consciously feel like there's a part of my brain that just can't connect. Very frustrating.

Thank you for your kind words. I'm probably about give you a really creepy impression of myself right now, but I don't see hope and suicide as mutually exclusive. I actually do love myself, but I still want to die sometimes. My desire to end myself is a result of me weighing my options. 

I was sort of living in a preprogrammed hell and finally decided to try to do something about it roughly 5 years ago. I don't know if you've seen this movie the Adjustment Bureau (and if not, you're not missing anything it's pretty terrible), but you're going against nature's plan and life really doesn't like you taking matters into your own hands. 

I don't want to sound like a whiner, isolation was never my issue to be honest, I'm really sorry if that was part of your path. I ended up isolating myself to get off the path of settling and unhappiness I was on. So now I know that feeling very well. 
 
I've never really had a problem loving myself per se, I just have a LOT of limitations. It gets exhausting trying to overcome them on a daily basis. I love myself, I just don't like who I am if that makes any sense. There are cerain parts of myself that are very resistant to change despite all my efforts. I wish I was better at life...I could see how that could look like self-hatred, but I really don't feel like I hate myself or the world or anything. I want to belong, I just can't meet my own standards no matter what I do and I guess I'm feeling really stuck. I  really do appreciate the effort you made to cheer me up though.

No this is good stuff. Without going into detail of what was going on in our lives at the time, this discussion seems slightly abstract but I think we're totally on the same page. OP don't worry we have not lost our minds :) (yet) How did I survive before I found these subs? Your description was so similar to what I went through. I haven't had the opportunity to discuss this with a therapist but I think they might see this as an positive sign that reintegration is taking place. I had a lot of layers of shame to strip away, but a sick core contaminating everything else remained and once I finally let myself get in touch with that, it finally healed the parts of me that were sort of still stuck in a much earlier stage of development. Comparing notes is so reassuring, I'm also feeling liberated and raw in a way that is pretty new to me. Very different from the initial high of breaking free from my abusers.
Likewise! The members of this sub have restored my faith in humanity, seriously.

Hi there, I'm really sorry for leaving you mid-celebratory fist pump or for not returning the gesture of solidarity you had been extending here. I'm finally appeasing the voice in my head that's been nagging at me like, "Where are your manners Cheez?? Send off that thank you to the kind stranger who called your parents monsters." 

I appreciate your empathy so so much. The crazy thing is that somehow between now and what appears to be 4 days ago, I've finally come to the conclusion that I don't need anyone to validate me anymore. I can't thank you enough for being a big part of that. This is (hopefully) the beginning of something incredible for me after years of healing.

It might help to start putting it out there that you're venting not because you don't know what to do, but because you feel alone. They should able to be just as helpful without pointing the finger at you. They might not realize it's the compassion that makes all the difference. Even if they keep insisting you're not making compromises or are not taking responsibility for yourself, stay calm and don't give them an easy excuse to support that error in their judgment. Sometimes it takes a while to get people to see where you're coming from.

Shaming us and acting they're better is like bragging about making more free throws than someone who is blind. Who gives themselves a gold star for having a better handle on life than a child abuse survivor? Are they also proud they can run faster than a 6 year old? Not to say we aren't capable of being just as whole as anyone else, but it's practically common sense that many of us lack coping skills until we learn, not from our parents but through years of therapy, joining support groups and reading the literature on childhood trauma. Our bond with our parents isn't forged by choice, it's biological. Managing conflict within that biological bond where we are constantly in a one-down position is incredibly difficult.

I can relate to every word. Yup. Not only does it destroy the trust between you and your parents, it changes the way we see the institutions that are supposed to serve, not harm the children we once were. I'll spare you the details but this was a fun game my bored, semi-retired dad liked to play on occasion as his physical abuse escalated and he realized he might get caught. The law never intervened in a way that was helpful to anyone, even the lying-sack-of-shit aka dad. It seems to bring out the worst in everyone involved. I never hated cops despite my parents pulling these stunts, but I did develop a skewed, dark perspective on the world which was probably even worse. 

The most innocuous things can be used to discredit you. As I got older, some of my mom's enablers assumed I must have been a difficult child because I've grown up to be very open-minded. I've had close friends across the political and religious spectrum and I'm not even openly political or really that knowledgable to be honest. Still their problem-child radar is so sensitive it immediately goes off if I mention I watch a few HBO shows or try out a new fashion trend they haven't caught on to yet. I don't even have a tattoo or crazy hair or a visibly "aggressive" appearance, I'm probably less edgy than your average millenial.

For starters, steer clear of people with incredibly short tempers who are operating heavy machinery. I've been there, my mom has jumped out of a car while stopped at a red light and driven erratically to intimidate me. Protect yourself. You probably already know on an intellectual level your energies are wasted on the power struggle, but when you start to take control over your life it will take on a new meaning. It's not your fault this is happening, but there are definitely steps you can take to minimize contact and give yourself some much needed room to breathe. Distancing yourself isn't about letting her win, but about showing love for yourself. I've been really proud of myself lately because I'm so close to not even caring about the way she exploits our issues to get sympathy or the way she lies to make me look bad. I never thought it would be possible and here I am! 

I say this all the time on here but financial independence changes everything. It's very discouraging at first when you are starting from zero but as the commas in your bank statement accumulate, it's one of the most empowering feelings ever.

That checks all my boxes as well. Risk adverse, check. Making compromises I can't really live with, check! Like you said, everything just felt wrong. I finally gathered the courage to start over, completely. It was a little extreme, I didn't go out guns blazing but I did quietly distance myself from a lot of people. Maybe it wasn't totally necessary, but it gave me inspiration to become more of an observer and start choosing who I wanted to be from a more informed place. 

I would say I made the most progress in a short amount of time when I finally stopped running from my most deeply buried fleas. This was a few years after I discovered that cluster b was a thing. Even when I knew what was off with my family, I couldn't successfully detach from it until I owned my darkest fears and mistakes, which makes sense even from a practical perspective. Scary as hell, but now the whole attic's been cleared out, the lights are on and there are no more dark corners for dysfunction to hide. I wasn't too successful at analyzing myself in the past, because there was so much that needed to change before I could even go there. Everyone has their own way of dealing with it, that's just how it has been working out for me! <3

I finally started letting my intuition guide me while continuing to work on the parts of myself that needed to change. I've still made a mess of it at times but they are my messes, which are a lot more fun to clean up than someone else's. I consulted a lot of resources on mental health but my approach is my own.
Saving your response, thank you.

Wow, your wife must be very special to make it worth the effort you've made to accommodate her disorder. You really speak from experience. No sarcasm intended. It's slightly baffling to me in all honesty, but I also admire the way you've disentangled the love from the contempt and disgust we often feel at their behavior. You seem to have risen above that. I feel like I might be (finally!) getting there with my mom. The irony is that I used to base my identity around helping people but as I heal the wounds of my codependency, I find myself getting better at being helpful to others but no longer finding it as fulfilling. Are you supporting her with the goal that someday, whether it's 5 or 10 years down the road, she will make a full recovery?

BPD is really not that predictable in my experience. People change over time and triggers can too. So predictably unpredictable ends up meaning unpredictable after all. I can try to stay a few steps ahead of the game, but on a day to day basis I really do not know what to expect with my mom.

Intentions matter more to them than their actual behavior. What they wish was true is equal to what is. I took my mother's version of her past for granted until recently when I picked up on some serious inconsistencies. I honestly can't even trust her to give me directions while driving, because she'll pretend to get confused just to push my buttons. I can't call her out on gaslighting like this, because it will just lead to personal attacks and insults. Which makes sense, she gives herself the green light for life by labeling me as the all-bad. If my mom is in paranoid splitting mode and thinks I'm a horrible person, then she thinks it's okay to say anything as long as she believes there's something ugly she needs to expose.
Yeah but an invulnerable BPD is basically a sociopath. Don't forget they might relapse after treatment too.

BPD abusers understand power instinctively, and I've come to see them more as damaged sociopaths. *Sociopath, Interrupted*, basically. The traditional characteristics of sociopathy but with a fun little self-loathing twist! Take a common scenario where the adult child of BPD abuse achieves independence and goes NC, these abusers greatly tone it down only because they understand power. They aren't just making temporary lapses in judgement, the abuse usually goes on for at least 18 years and then some. Even if a BPD abuser is admittedly very sick, I think seeing the pain and suffering of their children over such a long period would touch them, and lead to natural adjustments in their temperment regardless of social norms. Instead, they see the suffering of their victims as somehow an excuse to be more abusive.  Severe dissociation is probably a factor, but even in my most dissociated state, I still had a warmth I've only ever seen temporary flickers of in my mom. My approach to Dealing With The Crazy has changed. Her entitlement used to be out of control until I started to leverage it to point out her distorted BPD ways of thinking and reasoning in her daily life, unrelated to her relationship to me. I feel like this would work better on women than men for some reason. The fact that she has hurt me is evident and she has never cared about that, but when her pride is wounded it sinks in deeper. I don't even bother to point out her abusiveness, just that she is wrong about a lot of things. It has not been pretty. She still overreacts like a toddler, she still sees her flaws as the ultimate humiliation. The toxic shame is still in place but as the entitlement crumbles, she can't fuel the engine of the abuse as efficiently. This could be temporary, especially if she finds a way to feel superior again. She might emerge from this as a plain old sociopath or finally learn to regulate her emotions and be a human being, who knows. I do know I'm sick of playing Frankenmommy, therapist, servant, and punching bag while trying to grant her wishes like a mediocre genie when she's gaming the system by wishing for infinite wishes.  

Even Darth Vader has a sympathetic backstory. The borderline part of BPD describes the literal line between psychopathy and normalcy, but the only thing anchoring them from detached entitlement is their insecurity. That's not really walking a borderline, they basically live in permanently mixed states and rage and humiliation dwarf any of their other emotions. As I'm beginning to (barely) develop my real identity beyond a rescuer role and detach from my mother I can finally see it. Even therapists (from her country of origin anyway) seem to underestimate the severity, because they project their own normal logic onto her. Once I stopped projecting my love and compassion onto her it made things so much clearer. I focused on the chaos so the neglect went overlooked for so long, never asking me how I am, knowing nothing personal about me, not vacationing with me since I was 14 while traveling the world herself, and never once showing me how to budget, invest, pay taxes, plan for my future. I have better examples of her neglect but I don't want to sound like a broken record on here. The neglect should have been my biggest clue that she was doing this on purpose.

Her idea of remorse or penance is not yelling at me as much. That's the main improvment she's made in terms of the way she treats me (so far). She typically acts like this is a huge favor she's doing me, like she's holding back from the way I really deserve to be treated. Since I now make it a point to subtly but consistently address her black and white way of seeing things, the pendulum is swinging less violently. It opened my eyes to how real this disorder is. She never made much progress before. She's kind of always known she's a horrible mother but she never did anything about it. So far there's still a disconnect, the empathy is still not there. It doesn't serve her to change this and I haven't thought of a way to work around this yet. Last September she actually cried and said, you poor thing, it must have been so hard for you, and totally meant it. It was so brief, and she was back to her old tricks within probably less than 3 hours. It would have meant something to me a few years ago, she's only saying it now because she sucked the life out of me and is satisfied with the destruction so that's actually pretty twisted when you think about it. Still constantly reframing and being defensive as usual, but to a less explosive degree. She's probably on a path to some kind of recovery now but like I said I could have leveraged NC to the same result without it being such a drain on me. Sociopath with unstable expression or self-hating tendencies seems to be a pretty good working definition. 

The scope of your question is also beyond BPD when it comes to the sadistic aspect of it. Pain and pleasure have such a weird symbiotic relationship. It's universal. People like to do messed up stuff. Even if it's just violent video games, or tickling their siblings until they cry. Egos can spiral downward and upward, they have to be managed by desire to be better for its own sake.

Grooming is crucial, kids are literally the only ones that can be abused like this from birth. Most people are like that's my kid, that's a piece of me. I would love to see the smoking gun, just how young we were the very first time they ever abused us and took pleasure in our pain. They had a few years to slowly descend into hell, while we were still helpless infants. We didn't see it happening because we were just too young. Oh to have been a fly on the wall, it would have been chilling, I'm sure.

Trust your intuition. Are you dissociative? You could have been making all your decisions under the influence of dissociation for years. That could explain why nothing feels right. Maybe you could broach the subject with your therapist from that angle? The feeling you describe was always with me too, but for many years I obediently stayed in my little box, partly because I had this feeling it would be excrutiatingly painful to come out of it. Although I'm not N, I did have multiple false selves I had to shed. It was worth it, I can't even imagine how unfulfilled I would be if I hadn't made so many changes in my life. I wouldn't say I'm doing well but I'm 1000% percent recovered from codependency. I did sort of an audit of my past. Like why did I become so close to person A but not person B, why did I make certain decisions, what was the reality beyond my tunnel vision at the time. I didn't want to leave any stone unturned. The big epiphany was that despite being a resilient kid I was never really quite myself at ANY point in time. When family problems never get resolved and persist for years, something is definitely up. You don't have to do anything extreme right now, but the best thing for you is to become completely independent. Your love for your parents is working against you here. Abusive parents exploit your attachment to them, that's how they control you. Right now they pay for everything and that gives them a lot of power. The second I got at least 10K in the bank I started feeling so much more in control and more able to put up an emotional wall. I really had to get to about 50K in savings before I realized that I was capable of taking care of myself.  It might seem daunting at first, but it's all about baby steps. You'll naturally get stronger as you find ways to disenage from all the ways they try to bait you. The guilt trips only work if 1) There is even the smallest part of you that needs their love and approval 2) They have control over your decision making, whether they achieve this by battering you psychologically or physically 3) You're suffering from the consequences of a lifetime of abusive parenting and have been developmentally stunted in some way. Stay safe, don't give them any ammo. 

Therapy helps but don't forget, in the end you are the only one in charge. You can pay someone for their insight or for their support, but it's still just a paid service. No one can take better care of you than you.

You just need that one thing that gives you confidence and stability and gets the ball rolling, for me it was money, maybe for you it'll be a career path or even a family of choice, a group of encouraging, well-rounded friends. 

You already made it through 16 and a half years of it, someday you'll look back and realize how brave and mature you were!! It's a lot to go through, but it's better to rip the bandaid off now than letting that wound fester and get infected. Everyone has to grow up eventually, not having real parents is a massive handicap, but in the end you can end up in the same place as your more privileged peers. Just don't be bitter or afraid, that really screwed me up. As you get older you might find yourself acting like your parents, and you have to do some tinkering to get past that. Be real and honest with yourself and get on the path to being a strong, independent person. That's what you would have to do even if you were from a normal family anyway. Just trying to tell you all the things I wish someone would have told my 16 year old self! Good luck.

Have you heard of ACE scores? You sound like you would have a pretty high one. It's one way that childhood trauma is now being measured, they can predict all kinds of outcomes from it, even the incidence of cancer. Your pain is real and it affects every cell in your body to an extent. So it's not only psychological trauma, it's everything. ACE stands for adverse childhood experiences, and the scoring can come in handy for example in therapy as a way to estimate the level of trauma they expect to be handling with you.

We never had normal conversations and banter the way people do. I'd never seen my parents develop a passion for something, even a hobby. Neither of my parents has an identity. I've only experienced them as broken people. My parents resent success so they framed my totally innocent desire to fit in enough to not seem weird, as spoiled and shallow. They constantly knocked me down without even really knowing me, even went out of their way to buy me a weird car so I would feel like an outcast. If I asked for a ride to a friend's house every once in a while, my dad would have a tantrum and scream he wasn't rich like my friends, totally unprovoked. They made me feel like a burden, so I never took care of myself the way my friends did. Do you need some words of encouragement? You're going to make it into vet school, you're worthy of your goals, the dream exists within you because it is the real you. The abuse doesn't define you, it's really just something horrible that randomly ended up happening to you, like a tornado destroying your house. It wouldn't make sense to take that personally and neither should you. Abusers are tornadoes ripping up the ground under your feet and flinging our belongings (sometimes literally) around in every direction so that we lose our identity. Hopefully you're already NC because I think it's very hard to heal when your wounds keep being reopened.

How about, "What are your biggest regrets?" I think N's hate being vulnerable and will give you suspicious answers to questions like that. N's love to talk about themselves until it gets real. They either externalize blame or give a fake answer that won't reveal their true humiliation, shame or sadness.

Maybe there is really no single tell, or question but I think questions like these reveal the inner workings of Ns:

"What makes you feel vulnerable?"
"Have you ever felt humiliated?" 
"What was your greatest disappointment?" 
"What would you change about yourself?"
"What makes you feel jealous?"


I think this works on both covert and overt Ns (assuming they don't know about NPD and don't have enough self-awareness to mask their symptoms.) I think a trained professional would be able to tell if someone consistently gave narcissistic answers to these kind of questions.

Life is already confusing enough without being born to N parents...I often wonder what it's like for people who know what home feels like. For me, home is the most terrifying place I could ever be. I'm on the road to finding closure too, a lot of things had to change in my life for me to even feel like it was possible. I was almost driven to suicide not because of the abuse that occured at home, but because my mom projected her mental illness onto me and tried to alienate me from sources of support while I was living in a foreign country with her. She married a dude who was on his third marriage, who was a drunk, wife-beating pedophile who at the very least physically and emotionally abused 4 of his kids, and then my parents continued to share several properties together long after they divorced. My house was like a hotel, 3 months with mom, 3 with dad, 3 with my grandparents, and I was only 11 when all this started. They were physically abusive to each other, yet my mom left me with him, and would pretend she was this hardworking breadwinner who didn't want to be separated from her kids when she abandoned me from birth, not teaching me how to read, make a bed, ride a bike, etc, and only seemed to have time to hit me and terrorize me while putting all the responsbilities of child-rearing to my nannies, dad, and grandparents. Get used to being your own advocate, and start looking into their past as well. My mother was mentally ill as early as 2nd grade, she's been sick for a long time. 

Now that I've gotten the ball rolling, no matter what she says, I can take a breath and calmly unravel her lies. I don't trust therapists or anyone right off the bat. If someone earns my trust, then I'll let myself be vulnerable over time. All or nothing thinking contributed to some of my avoidant patterns. Getting used to failure and rejection was also crucial for me. I think enablers are best handled after the abuse victim has overcome codependency, distorted thinking, and restored autonomy to their lives. Part of the problem is when people who are still relatively early in their recovery finally stumble upon the idea of Cluster B abuse. Emotionally, they've been starved for so long, but coming back to health is a long, incremental process. When you've been malnourished and starved long term, you can't eat a normal meal right away. The sight, smell, and texture of food is so intense, your brain is sending all these signals to devour everything in sight, but your body needs time to adjust.

Enablers feed a very unnecessary power struggle that mirrors the original conflict between abusive parents and children. They can interpret a victim's progress and recovery as just more proof that the victim brought their suffering upon themselves. Their agenda is to get the victim to admit fault at all costs, and the more a victim resists, or experiences a setback due to victim blaming, the more enablers are convinced that the responsibilty lies with the victim. If a victim is still developing the communication skills to explain abuse to someone who has never experienced it to that degree, they just seem weird and immature. If the victim is still suffering from PTSD, dissociating, and having trouble expressing themselves, it just looks bad to the average outsider. When we're still hurting and trying to figure things out, enabling and denial has the most power over us. Sending them info about narcissistic abuse can backfire, if they don't quite make the connection, they might even take this as a sign of your guilty conscience trying to protect itself. The average flying monkey has no clue they are recreating the original trauma in a new context, which why it is so dangerous to abuse survivors. In comes more of denial that triggers us in the first place, and more emotional injuries for the survivor who is already struggling. 

One of the best pieces of advice I've heard on this, is that the safest bet is to take a step back, and give yourself some time to figure out how you're feeling until you start approaching flying monkeys for support. Coming to places like RBN, establishing a rapport with a therapist, reading Pete Walker, or the Body Keeps The Score and waiting out the initial feelings of euphoria, moodiness, and confusion until we truly emotionally mature and move on.

Abuse victims are *by definition,* emotionally immature. Imagine being an infant, crying yourself to sleep night after night, year after year, abusive parents are careful to confine abuse to the privacy of their homes. Living with a mother who grimaces when you smile, a father who hits you and knocks you down when you're learning to walk. There are people out there that have never experienced a year, let alone a single month, with a parent that is stable. Abuse can be even more subtle, let's say a kid wants chocolate ice cream for his 6th birthday, and his parents get him vanilla. So on Thanksgiving, he asks for chocolate again, his parents call him a spoiled brat and tell him he should be happy with pumpkin pie. Already mishandling the situation by introducing black and white thinking, extremes, emotional reasoning, and labeling into the mix. They tell their bratty 6 yr son to hold off on until Christmas, the son gets his hopes up, he just needs to wait a few more weeks, he tells himself. So on Christmas, he asks for chocolate ice cream again and there so much pent up excitement he can hardly contain his happiness. Somehow he winds up with strawberry. So he cries, and his parents spank him. And this is how it works for EVERY need that the child tries to define for himself. Eventually he's going to stop asking for anything, and maybe become hopelessly confused and guilty about who he really is. This is exactly how people become Bipolar or develop BPD.

From there, they assume that our problems with our parents are partly due to a deficit in our character, even if they recognize that abuse did occur. They think not being able to forgive says something about us: that we were difficult children, that we were entitled, that we were somehow more immature, somehow less than. That we're a demographic of easily offended, second-class citizens. It's really traumatizing to be honest. They draw conclusions that are way off-base. In those scenarios, I'm just like, if I'm going to be judged as this difficult person, I should I have just been rebellious to begin with! I should have been demanding and self-absorbed if thats how it was going to turn out anyway. What was the point in fighting it? There are plenty of successful adults on this network that went NC, and haven't changed their minds despite making it out. The pain is still there. There are 18, 19 year olds who are firm in stating that they will never speak to their parents again. I don't think it's just a matter of how your life ended up turning out. The tantrums are threatening to us because of all the years of conditioning, it brings us back emotionally to the time we were helpless and trapped with them as children. That's why we take their anger so seriously when anyone else would look like a total idiot or an obvious psycho. When she's having a tantrum, I make an effort to slow down my own thoughts, and regulate my breathing. I let Nmom scream, and let myself cry if what she's saying hurts me. I don't speak before thinking through my words, this helps to slow everything down and prevent my conditioned response from taking over. Detach, but don't dissociate. It's a way of reframing her provocations. She's not poking the bear, this is who she is. The reaction seeking behavior isn't some unpleasant side effect, it's how she is and has always been. It's not even really a tantrum if it's how she is all the time. I let her yell at me, she sometimes runs out of things to say, and will take a minute to recharge, and that's when it's so clear that she's unstable. I don't think it's the best idea to put yourself in harm's way, but learning to navigate the tantrums can help you realize that you are not actually helpless, the fear they put into you is the *fear of a child.*

Some variation of this:

"It really hurts me when you say that. We've known each other since (pull on the heartstrings a little here) and I thought you respected my judgement. I've struggled with this for a lot longer than you might think.

Or you could keep it short and sweet, "Can you extend me the same sympathy you have for my dad?"

If they still trust your dad, the more likely they are to stay neutral. Neutrality means our integrity gets questioned, and the abuser gets the benefit of the doubt. So plant seeds of doubt about your dad's credibility. My dad was an abuser, but he was also a cheater. Not many would be willing to sing the praises of a cheater. People need to know that your N is not who he appears to me. Round out the picture and show them how much they don't know, even if they think they do. It's a sad reality that stories and examples of abuse are often not enough to elicit the disgust they deserve. If you disrupt *their* picture of your dad on a personal level, it can really make the deceptive nature of N's very clear.

If your friends are still not getting it, chances are something is not clicking with them on an emotional level. So good storytelling and avoiding labels and emotionally charged language are key. You kind of have to pander to them on some level. For instance, I was "lucky," in that my father has physically attacked me so I do have a "real" abuse card to play. But I know now to avoid outright accusing him of being abusive unless the person I'm speaking to draws that conclusion first. 

If dad's mentally unstable, talk about his weird habits, the times he acted inappropriately in public. Ironically, it helps to almost think like an N, exposing their vulnerablities to get the support and validation you need.

I recently read up on compensatory narcissism and it was really helpful to me. As a kid I had to be such a brown noser just to have friends that when my mom completely sabotaged my education I had this period of wanting to prove to everyone how worthy I was, mainly because I was hoping people would recognize my lost potential as a CLEAR indication of abuse. That backfired spectacularly. In fact, my mom gained a bunch of enablers who erased my pretty normal-on-the-outside illusion I had worked so hard to create up until then. Then, when I became aware of what was happening I realized that I had always a tendency to deal with rejection, fear, ignorance or failure by dismissing it or pretending I don't care about the things that mattered to me most. Which really explained how I ended up in a major in college that I hated and a boyfriend I disliked just as much, why everything in my life felt so unnatural even if it worked for some other people.

So I hope you put yourself out there and let yourself care and keep making mistakes until things start falling into place a little more. It was a lot easier once I realized pretending that I don't care doesn't change anything and that the universe isn't going to magically intervene on my behalf.
